# Kestrel field guide

## Identification

Hovering into the wind with its head held perfectly still is the most reliable field mark. Migrants arrive on the first southerly winds of spring and leave again by late September. Incubation lasts about a month, and the young leave the nest some four weeks after hatching.

## Habitat

The kestrel hunts over open moorland and is most active in the two hours after sunrise. Survey teams count the kestrel along fixed transects, walking slowly and recording every bird seen or heard. Plovers run in short bursts and stop abruptly, tilting forward to pick prey from the sand. The kestrel nests on ledges and in old crow nests; it lays four to six eggs in late April.

Numbers fall after hard winters, when snow cover hides the voles the birds depend on. Owls are counted at dusk by listening for territorial calls from fixed points along the valley. Record weather, tide and observer name at the top of every survey sheet. Migrants arrive on the first southerly winds of spring and leave again by late September. Plovers run in short bursts and stop abruptly, tilting forward to pick prey from the sand. Herons stand motionless in shallow water for long minutes before striking at a fish.
